section.title: The Wisdom of the Spirit
section.sectionRationale: Paul now shows the cross-shaped pattern in his own ministry and then explains how anyone comes to grasp the wisdom of the cross at all. He came not with eloquence but in weakness, resolved to know only Christ crucified, so that faith would rest on God's power. True wisdom is real, but it is the hidden wisdom of God, unknown to the rulers of this age who crucified the Lord of glory, and it is revealed only by the Spirit who searches the deep things of God. The natural person cannot receive it; but those who have the Spirit have the mind of Christ.
section.thesis: The wisdom of God centered in Christ crucified is hidden from human wisdom and from the rulers of this age, and can be received only through the Spirit who searches the depths of God; the natural man rejects it as folly, but those who have the Spirit are given the very mind of Christ.
section.frameNote: Four movements: Paul's plain preaching in weakness, resting faith on God's power; the hidden wisdom of God ordained before the ages; the Spirit who alone reveals the deep things of God; and the natural man against the spiritual man who has the mind of Christ.

verses.text: When I came to you, brothers, I did not come with eloquence or wisdom as I proclaimed to you the testimony about God.
For I resolved to know nothing while I was with you except Jesus Christ and Him crucified.
I came to you in weakness and fear, and with much trembling.
My message and my preaching were not with persuasive words of wisdom, but with a demonstration of the Spirit’s power,
so that your faith would not rest on men’s wisdom, but on God’s power.

units.label: The hidden wisdom of God
units.note: ordained for our glory before the ages

verses.text: Among the mature, however, we speak a message of {{sophia|wisdom}}, but not the wisdom of this age or of the rulers of this age, who are coming to nothing.
No, we speak of the {{mysterion|mysterious}} and hidden wisdom of God, which He destined for our glory before time began.
None of the rulers of this age understood it. For if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory.
Rather, as it is written: “No eye has seen, no ear has heard, no heart has imagined, what God has prepared for those who love Him.”

units.label: Revealed by the Spirit
units.note: the Spirit searches the deep things of God

verses.text: But God has revealed it to us by the {{pneuma|Spirit}}. The Spirit searches all things, even the deep things of God.
For who among men knows the thoughts of man except his own spirit within him? So too, no one knows the thoughts of God except the Spirit of God.
We have not received the spirit of the world, but the Spirit who is from God, that we may understand what God has freely given us.
And this is what we speak, not in words taught us by human wisdom, but in words taught by the Spirit, expressing spiritual truths in spiritual words.

units.label: The natural and the spiritual man
units.note: but we have the mind of Christ

verses.text: The {{psychikos|natural}} man does not accept the things that come from the Spirit of God. For they are foolishness to him, and he cannot understand them, because they are spiritually discerned.
The spiritual man judges all things, but he himself is not subject to anyone’s judgment.
“For who has known the mind of the Lord, so as to instruct Him?” But we have the {{nous|mind}} of Christ.

sophia.gloss: Wisdom, insight, skill. Paul insists that the gospel is not anti-intellectual: there is a true and profound wisdom in it. But it is not the wisdom of this age or its rulers, which is passing away; it is the hidden wisdom of God, centered in Christ crucified and known only by the Spirit.

mysterion.gloss: A mystery, a truth once hidden and now revealed by God. It is not a puzzle to be solved by cleverness but a secret purpose that God alone can disclose. The wisdom of the cross was ordained before the ages and hidden from the rulers of this age, and is now made known through the Spirit to those who love God.

pneuma.gloss: Spirit, breath, wind; here the Holy Spirit of God. The Spirit alone searches and knows the deep things of God, just as only a person's own spirit knows his thoughts. God's wisdom is therefore not reached by human insight but revealed by the Spirit whom believers have received, so that they can understand what God has freely given.

psychikos.gloss: Natural, unspiritual, belonging to the merely human soul apart from the Spirit. The natural person, however intelligent, cannot receive the things of the Spirit; they seem foolish and remain closed to him because they are discerned only by the Spirit. The word marks the great divide Paul draws between those with the Spirit and those without.

nous.gloss: Mind, understanding, the faculty of thought and perception. Paul's climactic claim is that believers have the mind of Christ. Through the indwelling Spirit, the people once unable to know God's thoughts now share the very understanding of their Lord, which no natural wisdom could ever attain.

basic.context: Paul reminds the Corinthians how he first came to them: not with impressive speech or worldly wisdom, but resolved to preach only Christ crucified, and in weakness and trembling, so that their faith would rest on God's power rather than on his eloquence. Then he explains that the gospel really is wisdom, but a hidden wisdom that the world and its rulers missed, so that they crucified the Lord of glory. This wisdom is known only because God reveals it by His Spirit, who alone knows the depths of God. The natural person cannot grasp it, but those who have the Spirit have the mind of Christ.
basic.hermeneutics: Paul weaves his personal example together with teaching about revelation. He argues that the wisdom of the cross is real but must be given by the Spirit, and he supports this with Scripture, Isaiah on what God has prepared and on the mind of the Lord. The enduring point is that saving understanding is a gift of the Spirit, not an achievement of human intellect.
basic.originalLanguages: There is a true sophia, wisdom, but it is God's hidden wisdom, a mysterion, mystery, once concealed and now revealed. It is disclosed by the pneuma, the Spirit, who searches the depths of God. The psychikos, natural, person cannot receive it, but believers, given the Spirit, have the nous, the mind, of Christ.
basic.typology: The Spirit revealing the hidden wisdom of God fulfills the promise of God pouring out His Spirit on His people so that they know Him. The Lord of glory crucified by the rulers of this age fulfills the pattern of the rejected one whom God vindicates, as in the stone the builders rejected. What was hidden in the prophets is now unveiled in Christ by the Spirit.
basic.christ: Christ crucified remains the center: the one thing Paul resolved to know, and the Lord of glory whom the rulers failed to recognize and so crucified. The passage ends with the astonishing claim that believers have the mind of Christ, sharing His very understanding through the Spirit.
basic.god: God is the source of true wisdom, which He ordained before the ages for the glory of His people. He alone can reveal the depths of Himself, and He does so by His Spirit, who knows the thoughts of God as a person's spirit knows his own. Salvation and understanding alike are God's gift, freely given.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah speaks of what God has prepared for those who love Him. Jesus thanks the Father for hiding these things from the wise and revealing them to little ones. John promises the Spirit who guides into all truth. Romans cites the same question, who has known the mind of the Lord.
basic.oneStory: God's saving plan, centered in the cross, was hidden through the ages and is now revealed by the Spirit to those who love Him. What no human wisdom could discover, God freely gives, so that His people share the mind of Christ. The story moves from a wisdom hidden in God to a people indwelt by the Spirit and united to the Lord of glory.

context.literary:
First Corinthians 2 is the middle panel of a three part argument about wisdom that runs from 1:18 to 3:23. Chapter 1 sets out the paradox: the cross looks like folly and is God's power. Chapter 2 turns from the message to the messenger and then to the hearer. Paul first shows how the paradox shaped his own preaching, verses 1 to 5. He then explains why the wise of this age missed it, verses 6 to 9, and why believers do not, verses 10 to 16. Chapter 3 then applies the whole argument to the Corinthian factions.

The passage is built on a series of contrasts that Paul keeps pairing: eloquence and a demonstration of the Spirit, human wisdom and God's power, this age and the age before time began, the rulers who did not understand and the Spirit who searches everything, the spirit of the world and the Spirit who is from God, the natural person and the spiritual person. Almost every verse sets one pole against the other, so that the reader is made to choose a side.

Verses 10 to 12 form a small argument from analogy. In the same way that only a person's own spirit knows the thoughts within him, only God's Spirit knows God's thoughts. Paul then reasons forward: the Spirit knows God, we have received that Spirit, so we can know what God has given. Verse 13 turns this into a rule for speech, and verses 14 to 15 state the two possible responses. The unit is capped by an Old Testament question and a bold answer. Isaiah asks who has known the Lord's mind; Paul replies, 'But we have the mind of Christ,' verse 16.

Notice, too, where the passage sits in Paul's own story. The 'I' of verses 1 to 5 is the Paul who has just come from Athens, and the way he describes his arrival in 'weakness and fear, and with much trembling' stands in deliberate tension with the confident, plural 'we' of verses 6 to 16.
context.historical:
Paul founded the Corinthian church around AD 50 to 52, staying a year and a half, Acts 18:11. He arrived after Athens, where he had preached to philosophers on the Areopagus, Acts 17:22-34, and where the response was mixed. When he reached Corinth he found a different audience, but the same appetite for clever speech. Corinth had been refounded as a Roman colony in 44 BC. It was a wealthy, ambitious port city, and it prized self made success. It also prized rhetoric. Travelling speakers charged fees, gathered followers and competed for applause, and a speaker was judged by polish and presence.

Paul's critics at Corinth turned this standard on him. He later records the complaint, 'His letters are weighty and forceful, but his physical presence is unimpressive, and his speaking is of no account,' 2 Corinthians 10:10. Verses 1 to 5 read like an answer given in advance. He did not fail to be impressive; he chose to be plain, because the message was a crucified man, and a crucifixion was the most shameful form of execution that Rome used. To a Roman or a Greek, a crucified saviour was a contradiction.

The phrase 'rulers of this age' would also have carried weight. Most Corinthians had never met a Roman governor, but they lived under imperial authority and in a culture that honoured the powerful. Paul says those who held the most power in his generation did not recognise the Lord of glory when He stood before them, and that their ignorance is now plain, verse 8. Peter makes the same point about Israel's leaders, Acts 3:17, and Jesus prays for those who did not know what they were doing, Luke 23:34.

Finally, the word 'mature' in verse 6 was a loaded one in the religious culture of the day, where many cults and philosophical schools offered initiation into higher knowledge for the few. Paul uses the vocabulary but reverses its logic. The wisdom he speaks is given to all who have the Spirit, not to an elite who qualify by intellect or by rank.
context.canonical:
Paul's quotation in verse 9 is a woven phrase, not an exact citation. The BSB footnote points to Isaiah 64:4, 'From ancient times no one has heard, no ear has perceived, no eye has seen any God besides You, who acts on behalf of those who wait for Him.' Paul keeps the eye and the ear, adds the heart, and turns 'those who wait for Him' into 'those who love Him.' Isaiah 65:17, with its new heavens and new earth that will 'come to mind' no more as the old things do, may also lie behind the phrase about the heart. Isaiah 52:15 is close in spirit too: kings 'will see what they have not been told, and they will understand what they have not heard.' Paul reads these promises as already coming true.

The idea that God reveals what is hidden has a long root. In Daniel 2:22 and 2:28 God 'reveals the deep and hidden things' and 'reveals mysteries,' and the Aramaic and later Greek word behind 'mysteries' there is the same one Paul uses in verse 7. Daniel's mysteries concern what will happen in the latter days. Paul's mystery is that the latter days have arrived in Christ.

The role of the Spirit builds on Jeremiah 31:33-34, where in the new covenant God puts His law in people's minds and all know Him, and on Ezekiel 36:27, where God puts His Spirit within His people. When Isaiah 40:13 asks who has directed the Spirit of the LORD, the answer implied is nobody, and Paul finds the surprise: the Spirit whom nobody directs has been given to us.

The theme travels through the New Testament. Jesus thanks the Father for hiding these things from the wise and revealing them to little children, Matthew 11:25. In John 16:13-14 the Spirit of truth guides the disciples into all truth and takes from what is Christ's to disclose it to them. John tells his readers that they have 'an anointing from the Holy One,' and 'all of you know the truth,' 1 John 2:20. Ephesians 3:4-6 speaks of the mystery of Christ now revealed by the Spirit to the apostles and prophets, and Colossians 2:2-3 says that all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in Christ.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul is not delivering a lecture on epistemology. He is answering a church that has been grading its teachers by style, and he wants them to see that the style was never the point. He holds himself up as evidence: his plain speech was a decision made for the sake of their faith, verse 5, not a failure of skill. The purpose of the whole passage is to move the Corinthians' trust from persuasive people to the power of God.

He also wants to stop them hearing this as anti-intellectual. There is wisdom, he says, a real and rich wisdom that was planned before time began, verses 6 and 7. The Corinthians' mistake was not that they loved wisdom but that they looked for it in the wrong place. The first hearers were meant to leave the passage humbled and glad at once. Humbled, because no one reasoned their way to the cross. Glad, because the Spirit now lives in them, so that the deep things of God are not out of reach.

There is a pastoral edge as well. Some Corinthians probably thought their spiritual gifts and knowledge made them a superior class. Paul tells them that what they know, they received, verse 12, and the same point returns in 4:7. Everything that distinguishes the believer from the world is a gift, and gifts leave no room for boasting.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Verses 1 to 5 are Paul's own account of how he preached at Corinth. They are not a rule that every preacher must speak badly or avoid preparation; Paul himself reasoned and argued in the synagogue, Acts 18:4. The lasting principle is that no method may be allowed to stand in for the Spirit's power, and that the content of the message, Christ crucified, must never be traded for a more attractive one.

Verses 6 to 16 describe what is true of the Spirit's work and of the two kinds of hearer. They are not a licence to look down on people who do not yet believe, or to treat Christian maturity as a status. Paul's own sentences guard against that. The 'natural' person is described as someone who 'cannot understand,' not as someone beneath contempt, and the spiritual person 'judges all things' only because he has received what he did not earn.

Verse 15 in particular needs care. It is a statement about the believer's standing before God and the world's verdicts, not a claim that the believer is above correction by the church. Paul himself insists in the next chapter that he is accountable to the Lord, 4:3-4.

debates.question: Who are the 'rulers of this age' in verse 8?

views.label: Human rulers
views.case: Pilate, Herod and the leaders of Jerusalem are the natural reading. Peter says that the people and their leaders acted in ignorance, Acts 3:17, and the same ignorance is the point here: they did not understand. Paul's word for rulers is used of human officials elsewhere, as in Romans 13:3.

views.label: Demonic powers
views.case: Many of the early Christian writers took the phrase to mean the evil powers behind the age, who had no idea that the cross would be their own defeat. Paul speaks of such powers elsewhere, as in Colossians 2:15, where Christ disarms the rulers and authorities in the cross.

views.label: Both together
views.case: The cross had a human face and an unseen background, and the Gospels show Satan working through the actors, as in Luke 22:3 and John 13:27. This view holds that Paul's language is wide enough to include human governments and the unseen powers that stood behind them.

debates.bearing: On any reading Paul's emphasis is that the powers acting at the cross did not grasp what they were doing. The question affects how far the verse is a political statement, but it does not change its main claim that the cross was hidden wisdom.

debates.question: Who are 'the mature' in verse 6, and is Paul describing two tiers of Christians?

views.label: All who have the Spirit
views.case: In verses 14 to 16 the division is between those with the Spirit and those without, not between advanced and ordinary Christians. Paul has just said that Christ is made wisdom for every believer, 1:30, and in verse 12 'we have received' the Spirit. On this view 'mature' is simply a way of saying fully initiated believers, as in Philippians 3:15 where Paul counts 'all of us who are mature' together.

views.label: Believers who have grown
views.case: In 3:1 Paul tells the Corinthians that he could not address them as spiritual, but as infants. Hebrews 5:14 uses the same adjective for those who have trained their senses by constant use. On this reading verse 6 describes a wisdom taught to those who are ready for it, in contrast to the milk of 3:2.

debates.bearing: The first view fits the logic of verses 10 to 16 and the second fits the opening of chapter 3. Most readers hold both: every believer has the Spirit and so access to the wisdom, while the Corinthians' behaviour kept them from taking it in. Either way, Paul is not describing a secret inner circle.

debates.question: Does verse 14 mean the unbeliever is unable to respond to the gospel?

views.label: Total inability without God
views.case: Paul says the natural person 'cannot understand' because the things are spiritually discerned. For many Reformed readers this describes a real moral and spiritual inability that only the Spirit overcomes, in line with 2 Corinthians 4:4 and Ephesians 2:1.

views.label: A refusal rather than a lack of intelligence
views.case: Other readers stress the word 'accept' at the start of the verse and note that Paul preached to such people in order to persuade them. On this view the problem is the person's rejection of what sounds like folly, a stance God's Spirit can change through the preaching.

debates.bearing: Both views agree that conversion is the Spirit's work, not human cleverness, and that the gospel must still be preached. Paul's own method in the same chapter shows that he preaches in the expectation that the Spirit will use his words, verse 4.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 4 contains a word from the law court and the lecture hall. The BSB's 'a demonstration of the Spirit's power' translates apodeixis, a word from the language of argument, used for a proof that settles a case. Paul sets it against 'persuasive words of wisdom,' the polished speech of the rhetoricians. The surprise is that Paul claims a proof of his own, but the proof is not logical. It is the Spirit's power, seen in changed lives, in the faith of the Corinthians themselves. The Corinthians' own faith is the exhibit.

Verse 6 describes the powers of this age as 'coming to nothing.' The verb, katargeo, is in the present tense, so the sense is that they are in the process of being made ineffective. Paul uses the same verb in 1:28 for God nullifying 'the things that are,' and in 15:26 for the last enemy, death, which will be destroyed. The rulers are not falling away by accident; God is actively undoing them.

In verse 7 the wisdom was 'destined for our glory.' The verb, proorizo, is a compound of 'before' and 'to mark out,' and Paul uses it in Romans 8:29-30 for God's choosing of those He will conform to Christ's image, and in Ephesians 1:5 and 1:11 for His plan. 'Before time began' is literally 'before the ages,' and the footnote points out another way to read the earlier phrase, 'we speak God's wisdom in a mystery.' The mystery here is the gospel plan that was hidden until Christ and is now made known, as in Romans 16:25-26 and Ephesians 3:4-6.

The verb for 'searches' in verse 10, eraunao, means to investigate with care. It is used of God who 'searches our hearts,' in Romans 8:27, and of Christ who 'searches minds and hearts,' in Revelation 2:23. The Spirit's search of God's depths is not a search by someone who does not know. It is the thorough knowing of God by one who is God.

The word 'freely given' in verse 12 comes from charizomai, the verb related to charis, grace. Everything the Spirit lets us understand is grace, a gift, so understanding itself is grace.

The expression in verse 13, 'expressing spiritual truths in spiritual words,' is hard to translate because the verb, synkrino, can mean to combine, to compare or to interpret, and the adjective can be neuter (spiritual things) or masculine (spiritual people). The BSB footnote notes the alternative 'to spiritual people.' The possibilities all point the same way: the content, and the way it is spoken, both come from the Spirit.

The 'natural' person of verse 14 is psychikos, from psyche, the soul or life breath, and means someone who has only the ordinary human life with no further gift. Jude 19 describes divisive people as 'devoid of the Spirit,' and James 3:15 speaks of wisdom that is 'earthly, unspiritual, demonic.' The 'discerned' of verses 14 and 15 is anakrino, to examine and judge, the same verb Paul will use in 4:3-4 for being judged by human courts. Finally, in verse 16 'mind' is nous. Isaiah 40:13 in Hebrew speaks of the Spirit of the LORD, and the Greek Septuagint renders it with the word for mind, so Paul's move from Spirit to mind is already present in the way Isaiah was read.

typology.fulfillment: In Daniel 2 the wise men of Babylon cannot tell the king his dream, and Daniel says that there is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries, Daniel 2:28. The picture is of a hidden meaning that no human cleverness can reach and that God gives to His servant. In Paul it becomes bigger and more personal. The hidden thing is the saving plan fixed before the ages, the cross and its meaning, and the Spirit gives it not to one prophet at court but to every believer. The pattern also reverses in one respect: Daniel interpreted a dream about future kingdoms, but Paul speaks of the kingdom's King already crucified. The type falls short in that Daniel's revelation was partial and for a moment, while the Spirit's is a permanent indwelling.

The rulers of this age did not recognise the Lord of glory, verse 8. This matches the pattern of the stone the builders rejected that became the cornerstone, Psalm 118:22, which Jesus applies to Himself in Matthew 21:42, and Peter applies in Acts 4:11. In the psalm, the leaders of Israel fail to see the stone's worth. Paul's escalation is that the rejected one is the Lord of glory, a title that the Old Testament gives to God Himself, as in Psalm 24:7-10, and that the rejection was itself the means of the plan. The type falls short because the psalm's stone is a figure and the passage's Lord of glory is a person who dies.

typology.type: The Spirit given to all God's people, Jeremiah 31 and Joel 2
typology.fulfillment: Moses wished that all the LORD's people were prophets, Numbers 11:29, and Joel promised that God would pour out His Spirit on all flesh, Joel 2:28. Jeremiah 31:34 foretold a time when 'they will all know Me, from the least of them to the greatest.' Verse 12 states the fulfilment: 'We have not received the spirit of the world, but the Spirit who is from God.' The correspondence is that the whole community, not a few prophets, now has the Spirit. The escalation is that this Spirit searches the very depths of God and gives believers the mind of Christ. The type is not yet complete, since we still know in part, 1 Corinthians 13:12.

typology.type: Paul's weakness as a pattern of the cross
typology.fulfillment: Paul's arrival 'in weakness and fear, and with much trembling' is not an Old Testament type in the strict sense, but it follows the pattern of the cross. God's power goes where human power would not, in the form of a crucified man and of a trembling preacher. In 2 Corinthians 12:9 the Lord says that His power is made perfect in weakness, and in 2 Corinthians 4:7 the treasure is in jars of clay. The correspondence is between the shape of the message and the shape of the messenger. The pattern falls short because Paul's weakness only points to Christ's; it does not accomplish anything of redemption itself.

study.christ:
Paul gives Christ the title 'Lord of glory,' verse 8. In the Old Testament, glory is the visible weight and beauty of God Himself, and 'King of glory' is the name sung at the temple gates, Psalm 24:7-10. James uses the same title, 'our glorious Lord Jesus Christ,' James 2:1, which is literally 'the Lord of glory.' To say that the rulers crucified the Lord of glory is to say that they nailed the one who shares in the divine glory to a Roman cross. The paradox of the passage is that glory and shame meet in one person. Paul's own sermon on the cross is not a sermon about a martyr but about the Lord.

The passage also leads to Christ as the content of the hidden wisdom. Paul has just said that Christ 'has become for us wisdom from God,' 1:30. In Colossians 2:2-3 he says it again in other words: Christ is the mystery of God, 'in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.' So when Paul resolves to know nothing except 'Jesus Christ and Him crucified,' verse 2, he is not narrowing his subject. He is pointing to the one place where all of God's wisdom is found. Everything else he teaches in the letter, about marriage, worship, resurrection and money, is an unfolding of it.

The Spirit's work is tied closely to Christ. In John 16:14 Jesus says that the Spirit 'will glorify Me by taking from what is Mine and disclosing it to you.' This is what Paul describes in verses 10 to 13: the Spirit reveals not a body of secret knowledge but Christ and what He has given. That is why the Spirit and the cross are not rivals. A preaching that depends on the Spirit's power, verse 4, is a preaching of Christ crucified, verse 2.

The last sentence is the boldest. Isaiah's question, 'who has known the mind of the Lord?' expects the answer, no one. Paul says, 'But we have the mind of Christ.' By using 'Lord' for the one whom Isaiah called the LORD, he places Christ in the position of the God who cannot be instructed, and then says that His people share that mind. This is not a claim that believers know everything. It is a claim that they are united to Christ, that they see the cross as He sees it, and that they are being taught by His Spirit to think His thoughts after Him. The pattern that governs the Christian mind is the one that Philippians 2 describes, a mind that goes down into humility and obedience for the sake of others.
study.god:
The passage shows God as a God who has a plan older than time. The wisdom of verse 7 was 'destined for our glory before time began.' Nothing in the cross was a recovery from a failed plan or an emergency measure; it was determined before the ages. That gives the Christian a stable ground. History is not a sequence of accidents, and the worst moment in it, the crucifixion, was the centre of what God meant to do.

God is also the one who reveals. Paul does not describe Him as a distant being who waits to be found. 'God has revealed it to us by the Spirit,' verse 10. Revelation is God's own initiative, so the knowledge of God is grace through and through. Paul's description of the Spirit's role, searching 'even the deep things of God,' and knowing His thoughts as a person's spirit knows his own, shows that the Spirit shares fully in the divine life. It is one of the clearest places in the letters where the Spirit is described as having the knowledge that belongs only to God, and it presses toward the doctrine of the Trinity: the Father who plans, the Lord of glory who is crucified, the Spirit who searches and reveals.

The passage also holds a tension that is easy to miss. God is hidden and He is made known. The wisdom is hidden from the rulers and from the natural person, yet it is the plan 'for our glory.' God is not playing a game with the human race. The hiddenness belongs to the shape of the cross itself, since a God who saves through a crucified man will not be found by those who are looking for power and display. His hiddenness is the form His grace takes toward those who trust in their own wisdom.

God is generous. The Spirit has been given 'that we may understand what God has freely given us,' verse 12. The gifts are given, the understanding of them is given, and the words to speak of them are given, verse 13. There is no point at which the believer takes over from God and produces something alone.

For worship, this means that the proper response to the gospel is not pride in having grasped it but gratitude for being given it. Paul ends the thought in Romans 11:33 in the same spirit, 'O, the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God!' and goes straight to the question of verse 34, 'Who has known the mind of the Lord?' The honest answer is that we know it only because He has told us.

crossReferences.note: The source Paul draws on for verse 9. Isaiah praises a God who acts for those who wait for Him, whom no eye has seen. Paul keeps the language of eye and ear and says that what God has prepared for those who love Him is now disclosed by the Spirit. Reading Isaiah's setting, a prayer for God to come down, shows that Paul sees the cross and the Spirit as the answer.

The question quoted in verse 16. In Isaiah it comes in a passage about the greatness of God, who needs no counsellor. The BSB reads 'informed Him as His counselor' where Paul has 'instruct Him.' Paul uses it twice over: no one can teach God, yet through the Spirit believers have the mind of Christ.

A God in heaven reveals mysteries, and Daniel says so to a pagan king whose own wise men had failed. The Greek translation of Daniel uses the same word for mystery that Paul uses in verse 7. Paul treats the gospel as the great mystery that Daniel's God has now made known, no longer about coming kingdoms but about the King.

Jesus praises the Father for hiding 'these things from the wise and learned' and revealing them 'to little children.' The same pattern as 1 Corinthians 2, in the voice of Jesus Himself. Paul's account of the Spirit's revelation is rooted in what Jesus had already said about the Father's choice.

The Spirit of truth 'will guide you into all truth' and will glorify Jesus by taking from what is His and disclosing it. This is the promise whose fulfilment Paul describes in verses 10 to 13, and it explains why the Spirit's teaching always leads back to Christ and never beyond Him.

'You, however, have an anointing from the Holy One, and all of you know the truth.' John's words to a church troubled by false teachers echo Paul's claim that every believer has received the Spirit. The knowledge in view is not a secret doctrine but knowing the truth about Christ, and the whole community shares it.

The Spirit helps in weakness and intercedes with groans too deep for words, and the one who searches hearts knows the Spirit's mind. Paul's picture of the Spirit's knowledge of the deep things of God in 1 Corinthians 2 is matched here by the Spirit's knowledge of our deepest needs. The Spirit is thoroughly at home on both sides.

The mystery of Christ, not made known in other generations, now revealed by the Spirit to the apostles and prophets, and the content is that the Gentiles are fellow heirs. It shows what Paul means by a hidden wisdom revealed: not a mere set of ideas, but the inclusion of the nations in Christ.

'In whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.' This is the same claim as 1 Corinthians 1:30 and 2:2 in other words. The Corinthians were looking for wisdom in teachers and in speech. Paul says that it is all stored in Christ and that the way to find it is to know Him.

The history behind verses 1 to 5. Paul came to Corinth from Athens, worked as a tentmaker with Aquila and Priscilla, reasoned in the synagogue and then went to the Gentiles, and was told in a vision to keep speaking because the Lord had many people in the city. His weakness and fear were real, and so was the promise.

The criticism of Paul in the very city that read this letter: forceful letters, unimpressive presence, speech 'of no account.' It shows that the Corinthians did measure Paul by eloquence, and it explains why he spends so long in chapter 2 defending his plain preaching as a choice and not an accident.

The new covenant promise that God will put His law in minds and write it on hearts, so that all will know Him from the least to the greatest. Paul's claim that every believer has the Spirit and the mind of Christ is the fulfilment of this promise, and it removes any ground for ranking Christians by intellect.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a question about wisdom. In Eden the tree stood for the claim to decide good and evil without God, and the serpent promised that eating would make the woman and the man like God, Genesis 3:5. Humanity chose the road of its own wisdom, and the rest of Scripture follows the damage. Proverbs holds up the fear of the LORD as the beginning of wisdom, but even Solomon, the wisest king, ended in folly. Israel's leaders were by turns wise and foolish, and the prophets complained that the wise men had rejected the word of the LORD.

Into that story comes Paul's claim. The wisdom that the human race has been groping after is not a body of ideas to be learned. It is a person and an event. God had a plan from before time began, and it was hidden, not because He was withholding it from the world but because the world could not recognise it. The rulers of this age, with all their power, put the Lord of glory on a cross and in doing so carried out the plan they could not see.

The passage also answers a question that the Old Testament raises and does not settle. How will God's people ever know Him as He means to be known? Moses wished that all the LORD's people were prophets. Jeremiah promised a day when everyone would know God. Ezekiel promised a new heart and God's Spirit within. Paul says that day has come. Because the Spirit searches the depths of God and lives in believers, ordinary people in a Roman port city have the mind of Christ.

Looking forward, the story is not finished. Paul says that the rulers of this age are 'coming to nothing,' present tense, so the ending is already settled but not yet fully seen. Believers still know in part, 13:12. The day will come when the Lord brings to light what is hidden, 4:5, and when, as Revelation describes, the nations walk by the light of the Lamb, Revelation 21:23-24. In the new creation the hidden thing will be seen without a veil. The wisdom that was destined for our glory will become the glory itself.

For the one reading it, the movement is from Eden's grasped wisdom to Calvary's given wisdom to the new creation's seen wisdom. Every step is grace, and the Spirit is the pledge of the next one.

quiz.q: Why did Paul come to Corinth in weakness, resolved to know only Christ crucified?

options.text: So that their faith would rest on God's power, not on human wisdom.
options.note: Verse 5 gives the reason: faith grounded in God's power rather than eloquence.

options.text: Because he had nothing else worth saying to them.
options.note: He chose this focus deliberately; the cross is the heart of the message, not a last resort.

options.text: Because he was ashamed of the gospel.
options.note: He was resolved to preach it; the weakness was to magnify the message, not to hide it.

options.text: Because eloquence and wisdom are always sinful.
options.note: The issue is misplaced trust in rhetoric, not that speech or thought is evil.

quiz.q: What does Paul mean by the mysterious and hidden wisdom of God?

options.text: God's saving plan in the cross, ordained before the ages and now revealed by the Spirit.
options.note: Verses 7 and 10 describe a wisdom hidden then disclosed by God's Spirit.

options.text: A secret code only the most intelligent believers can decipher.
options.note: It is revealed to those who love God, not earned by intellect; a mystery is disclosed, not cracked.

options.text: A teaching so obscure that no one can really know it.
options.note: It is genuinely revealed by the Spirit, not left unknowable.

options.text: The accumulated wisdom of the philosophers of this age.
options.note: Paul contrasts it with the wisdom of this age, which is passing away.

quiz.q: How is the wisdom of God made known to believers?

options.text: God reveals it by His Spirit, who searches the deep things of God.
options.note: Verses 10 to 12 ground all understanding in the Spirit's revelation.

options.text: By careful study and superior human reasoning.
options.note: Study has its place, but Paul says the Spirit alone reveals the depths of God.

options.text: Through the teaching of the rulers of this age.
options.note: The rulers failed to grasp it and crucified the Lord of glory.

options.text: It cannot be made known to anyone at all.
options.note: God has revealed it to us by the Spirit.

quiz.q: Why can the natural man not accept the things of the Spirit?

options.text: Because they are spiritually discerned, and he lacks the Spirit who alone reveals them.
options.note: Verse 14 says such things seem folly and cannot be understood without the Spirit.

options.text: Because he is simply not clever enough to follow the argument.
options.note: The barrier is spiritual, not intellectual; even the brilliant cannot grasp them apart from the Spirit.

options.text: Because God has hidden them from everyone permanently.
options.note: They are revealed by the Spirit to those who love God, not hidden from all.

options.text: Because the things of the Spirit are actually foolish.
options.note: They only seem foolish to him; in truth they are the wisdom of God.

quiz.q: What astonishing claim does Paul make about believers in verse 16?

options.text: That through the Spirit they have the mind of Christ.
options.note: Believers share the very understanding of their Lord by the Spirit.

options.text: That they can fully comprehend God without any limits.
options.note: They have the mind of Christ, but this is a gift of the Spirit, not exhaustive knowledge of God.

options.text: That they no longer need Scripture or teaching.
options.note: The Spirit works through the word Paul speaks; it does not bypass revelation.

options.text: That they have earned wisdom by their own effort.
options.note: It is freely given by the Spirit, not achieved by human wisdom.

questions: Paul refused to lean on eloquence so that faith would rest on God's power. Where might your confidence be resting on human persuasion or personality rather than on God?
The rulers of this age missed God's wisdom and crucified the Lord of glory. How does this warn you against measuring truth by worldly power and prestige?
The wisdom of God is received only by the Spirit. How does this shape the way you read Scripture and pray before you try to understand it?
The natural person finds the things of God foolish. How can this deepen your patience and prayer for those who do not yet see the beauty of the gospel?
Believers are given the mind of Christ. What would it look like to trust that gift and think God's thoughts after Him in a decision you are facing now?

translationNotes.note: The Lord of glory is a striking title; applied to the crucified Jesus, it quietly confesses His deity, making the sin of the rulers all the graver.
This adapts Isaiah 64:4 (with echoes of Isaiah 65:17), on what God has prepared for those who love Him; Paul cites it to show the wisdom now revealed was long promised.
Natural man renders psychikos, the person living by the mere soul apart from the Spirit; it does not mean unintelligent, but unspiritual, lacking the Spirit needed to discern God's things.
The quotation is from Isaiah 40:13, who has known the mind of the Lord; Paul turns the rhetorical question into a claim that believers, by the Spirit, share the mind of Christ.
